g.title: Question formation
g.rule:
Good questions follow a few fixed patterns.

talk: Interview your partner for a job they would love. Ask at least six questions.
What is the strangest question you have ever been asked?

r.text:
Most applicants prepare for the obvious questions. They know why they want the job, and they can describe their strengths without blinking. What they are rarely ready for is the question that seems to have nothing to do with work.

One recruiter in Almaty always asks candidates what they had for breakfast. "I'm not being nosy," she explains. "I want to know whether they can make small talk with a stranger. Half our work is conversation."

Another asks how many windows there are in the city. Nobody knows the answer, and that is the point. He is interested in how a person thinks aloud, and in which follow-up questions they ask.

Do such questions work? Research suggests that a gut feeling formed in the first minute is hard to change. A foolproof method does not exist. Could you tell me what you had for breakfast?

Why does she ask it?
o: To check whether candidates can make small talk

ex.q: The windows question has a correct answer that candidates should know.
What does research suggest?
o: First impressions are hard to change

r.text:
When my aunt moved into her flat, the neighbours told her that the previous owner, a retired pianist, had died there. My aunt does not believe in ghosts, and neither do I. Nevertheless, something strange did happen.

Every night at about eleven she heard three notes on a piano. She does not own one. The neighbours don't either. She checked the radio, the television and her phone. The longer she listened, the more nervous she became.

A sceptical friend offered a theory: old pipes can sound musical. A plumber came. The pipes were fine, he said, and so was the heating.

The mystery was solved by a child. The boy upstairs had been given a toy keyboard, and his bedtime was eleven. "I do like a rational explanation," my aunt says. "Although the more I think about it, the less I understand why he always played the same three notes."

r.text:
Ten years ago, when people felt unwell, they waited to see whether it would pass. Now they reach for their phone. Doctors say that more and more patients have already diagnosed themselves before they walk into the surgery.

Dr Sadykova has been working as a GP for twenty years. "I've seen a real change," she says. "This morning a man came in who had been reading about rare diseases all night. He had a headache and a rash, and he was convinced it was something terrible. It was an allergy to washing powder."

She is not against online information. Patients who have been following good advice often recover faster. The problem is that the internet has never examined anyone.

Her rule is simple. If you have had a symptom for more than a week, or if it has been getting worse, make an appointment. "And please," she adds, "don't tell me what the forum said."

r.text:
Fashion has always had opinions about age. The young, we are told, can wear anything, while the middle-aged should choose something sensible, and the elderly should disappear into beige.

Not everyone agrees. In Seoul there is a group of retired men, all over seventy, who are photographed every weekend in beautiful tailored grey wool suits and bright leather shoes. They have become more famous than most models.

Meanwhile, the rules for the young are changing too. A scruffy old cotton hoodie used to be the uniform of the teenager. Today some of the smartest dressers at university are the students.

Designers have noticed. One brand now uses models aged from sixteen to eighty in the same campaign. "The old are our best customers," its director says. "They have the money, the time, and, frankly, the taste."

Perhaps the only real rule is this: wear what fits, and wear it as if you chose it.

talk: Tell the story of your best or worst journey by air, train or bus.
Are you a nervous traveller? What helps you?

r.text:
I had been travelling for nineteen hours when I boarded the last flight home. I had a boarding pass for seat 14A, by the window, and all I wanted was to sleep.

Somebody was already sitting there. He was about eighty, and he was looking at the clouds as if he had never seen any before. His daughter explained that he had not flown since 1975, and that he had been waiting for this day for months. Would I mind the aisle seat?

I did mind. I was so tired that I could hardly speak. But I took 14C.

The turbulence started over the mountains. It was such a rough descent that several passengers were praying. The old man was laughing. He had been a pilot, his daughter told me, and he had landed in worse.

When we disembarked, he shook my hand. I had not slept at all, and it was the best flight I had had in years.

r.text:
How short can a story be? According to a famous legend, a writer once won a bet by producing one in six words. Whether or not it really happened, the idea has never gone away.

Today thousands of people regularly publish six-word stories online. Some are funny. Others are quietly devastating. The best ones usually end with a twist that makes you read them again immediately.

Teachers have enthusiastically adopted the form. Students who rarely finish a page will happily write ten tiny stories in a lesson. They quickly discover that every word has to work hard, and that an adverb in the wrong place ruins the rhythm completely.

Unfortunately, brevity is not easy. Most first attempts are just sentences. A real story, even a tiny one, needs a character, a change and, ideally, something left unsaid.

Here is mine: "Finally learned her language. She'd left."

ex.q: How long is the story in the legend?

What does a real story need?
o: A character, a change and something unsaid

Dear grandchildren,

By the time you read this, I will have been dead for some years, and you will be living in a world I can only imagine.

I expect that the summers will have become longer. Perhaps you will be spending July in the north, as people in my day went south. I hope the droughts will not have destroyed the orchards I planted.

Will people still be burning fossil fuels? I would like to think that by 2060 the last coal station will have closed, and that children will be learning about smog in history lessons.

We were not stupid, you know. We simply believed that somebody else would be solving the problem next year.

This afternoon it is drizzling, the garden is humid, and I will be planting one more tree before dinner. By the time it is tall, I will have gone. I hope you will be sitting under it.

Your grandfather

r.text:
Ask people what frightens them and they will mention sharks, plane crashes and bungee jumping. Ask an insurance company what actually kills us, and the list is far less dramatic: cars, stairs and sofas.

Psychologists explain it like this. If a danger is rare and spectacular, we remember it. If it is common and boring, we ignore it. Unless something appears on the news, we assume it will not happen to us.

This has practical consequences. People will pay for travel insurance when they go skydiving, but they will not wear a helmet on a bicycle unless the law makes them.

The real risk-takers, it turns out, are not the people who jump out of planes. They check their equipment twice. They are the ones who text while driving, and who will see the doctor "as soon as work calms down".

If you want an adrenaline rush, take up climbing. If you want to live longer, take the stairs carefully.

Why do we ignore common dangers?

r.text:
In February a 58-year-old teacher went cross-country skiing alone. She told nobody where she was going, and she left her phone in the car.

An avalanche blocked the path behind her. If she had turned back ten minutes earlier, she would have reached the road. Instead she spent three nights in a shelter she dug in the snow.

Rescuers say she did almost everything right. If she had kept walking, she would have become exhausted and lost. If she hadn't had a thermos and chocolate in her rucksack, she would probably not have survived the first night.

She is less proud of herself. "If I were a sensible person, I'd have told my husband my route," she says. "If I had taken the phone, they would have found me in an hour."

Would she ski alone again? "If anyone asked me today, I'd say no. Ask me again in spring."

r.text:
A nurse who spent years caring for the elderly once kept a record of what her patients told her. Almost nobody said they wished they had worked harder.

The commonest regret was simple. People wished they had spent more time with friends. "If only I had picked up the phone," one man said. Many wished they had been brave enough to say what they really felt.

Younger people, interviewed for comparison, had different wishes. They wished they earned more, that their flat were bigger, that their boss wouldn't email them on Sundays. Their wishes were about the present, and mostly about things.

The nurse draws a gentle conclusion. "The old don't say 'I wish I'd had a better car'. They say 'I wish I'd gone to that wedding'."

It is an exhausting thought, and an inspiring one. Is there somebody you wish you had called this week? There is still time.

r.text:
When I moved to southern Spain, the first thing I had to get used to was the silence at three in the afternoon. Shops were shut. Streets were empty. I used to think the siesta was a myth for tourists. It is not.

At home I used to eat lunch at my desk in ten minutes. Here, lunch takes an hour and a half, and afterwards many people lie down. At first I couldn't get used to sleeping in daylight. I lay on the bed feeling guilty.

Now, two years later, I'm used to it. I'm also used to having dinner at ten and going to bed after midnight, which once seemed insane.

Researchers are divided about whether a nap is good for you. A short one seems to help memory; a long one can cause insomnia.

My mother visited last month. "You didn't use to be so relaxed," she said, yawning. By day three she was napping too.

talk: What music do you remember loving as a child? What do you tend to listen to now?

r.text:
You are brushing your teeth, and suddenly you notice that you have been humming the same four bars for an hour. Psychologists have a name for it: an earworm.

Almost everybody gets them. They tend to be songs with a simple melody and one unexpected jump, and they usually arrive when the mind is not busy. People often remember hearing the song in a shop that morning without having paid attention.

Trying to forget the tune rarely works. In fact, the more you try to stop thinking about it, the longer it stays. Researchers suggest listening to the whole song once, because the brain seems to want to finish it. Others recommend chewing gum, or learning to hum something else.

Musicians, interestingly, suffer more than the rest of us. A cellist in one study couldn't stop hearing a concerto she had failed to play well at sixteen.

It could be worse. Most people say they enjoy their earworms. They only regret choosing them so badly.

It started with a spoon. My brother had put a wet spoon back in the sugar. By the end of the evening we were arguing about a holiday in 2014.

A family therapist I later interviewed was not surprised. "The spoon can't have been the real problem," she said. "Somebody must have been feeling ignored for weeks."

She hears the same story every day. One partner should have said something months ago and didn't. The other might have noticed and chose not to. When the argument finally comes, it attaches itself to the first small thing available.

Her advice is practical. You shouldn't say "you always" or "you never". You should describe one event, and what you would rather happen next time.

I tried it. I told my brother that I'd rather he dried the spoon. He looked at me as if I had lost my mind. Then he said he would rather I didn't leave my shoes in the hall. We must have talked for two hours.

Professional card players spend years learning to control their faces. What they cannot easily control is everything else.

r.text:
Five years ago, bicycle theft was the commonest crime in a small Dutch-style university town. Hundreds were stolen every month, and almost none were recovered. Students had their bikes taken so often that many stopped buying them.

Then the council tried something unusual. A thousand yellow bicycles were bought, and they were left unlocked around the town. Anyone could take one. It was hoped that nobody would steal what was already free.

At first the scheme was laughed at. Within a month, two hundred bikes had been thrown in the river or sold. The council is said to have considered giving up.

Instead, each bike was fitted with a cheap tracker, and local teenagers were paid to repair them. Vandalism fell. Thefts of private bikes are reported to have dropped by half, although nobody is sure why.

The mayor has a theory. "A crime is easier to commit against a stranger," he says. "These bikes belong to everybody. They have been adopted."

r.text:
On a Tuesday in spring, a website reported that a well-known bakery chain was closing all its shops. By evening the story had been shared two hundred thousand times. It was not true.

A journalist decided to trace it backwards. The website admitted copying it from a blog. The blogger denied inventing it and blamed a post she had seen. r.text:
Every generation of scientists has believed things that the next generation found ridiculous.

For centuries, all educated people were sure that the Earth stood still. Every doctor recommended removing blood from patients, and most of them thought fresh air was dangerous. Neither idea survived proper experiments.

In the twentieth century, both sugar and fat were blamed for heart disease at different times, and no theory lasted more than a few decades. Any student who had suggested that stomach problems were caused by bacteria would have been laughed at. Two researchers proved it, one of them by drinking the bacteria himself.

At the end of the school year, one student is chosen to give a speech to the whole school. This year it was Dinara, who had never spoken in public and who describes herself as the quietest girl in the class.

She prepared for a month. A teacher gave her three pieces of advice. First, find a face in the audience and speak to it. Second, don't learn the speech by heart; learn the order of the ideas. Third, the first sentence matters more than the rest.
